correctness.rationale: Proposition 1.1 reduces s-practicality to exact prefix inequalities for the sorted positive values \(s(d)\). The proof exhausts every multiplicative partition of \(\Omega(n)=2,3,4\), uses the exact identities \(s(p)=1\), \(s(p^2)=p+1\), and \(s(pq)=p+q+1\), and leaves only eight explicit rejected candidates plus \(60\). Direct weight lists verify every terminal inequality, while \(60\) satisfies all prefix inequalities. A standalone finite replay through \(10^6\) agrees but is not used as proof.

originality.rationale: The inspected founding paper proves infinitude and density zero for s-practical numbers but does not classify them by prime-factor multiplicity. OEIS A393492 tabulates examples and records a prime-power exclusion, not the sharp composite threshold or uniqueness at \(\Omega(n)=4\). Focused published-finding searches returned adjacent but different notions of practicality and divisor subset sums, with no statement implying this theorem. The inaccessible 2026 thesis is retained as an explicit residual risk rather than treated as negative evidence.
residual_risks: The full text of Anniek Reuijl's 2026 master's thesis was not available for inspection. Because it studies representation by sums of proper divisors, it could contain an unindexed equivalent or stronger low-multiplicity result. Indexed metadata and OEIS expose only the no-composite-prime-powers consequence.
Search and indexing cannot logically rule out every differently phrased or unindexed equivalent statement.

value.rationale: The source introduces s-practical numbers as a natural nonmultiplicative practical-number analogue for which the usual structural machinery does not apply. The standard multiplicity invariant \(\Omega(n)\) asks for the first possible composite layer; the theorem gives the sharp global barrier and completely classifies equality, rather than an arbitrary bounded census. The unique boundary object \(60\) and the short exact obstruction list provide a reusable structural starting point for higher layers.
